newsitem.title: FRANCE: French film hero Kassovitz in rocky Cannes landing.
newsitem.headline: French film hero Kassovitz in rocky Cannes landing.

text.p: The Cannes critics who glorified France's fist-in-the-face director Matthieu Kassovitz have booed his new tale of a loser's initiation to murder whose subversive message fell flat.
Two years ago, when he was just 27 years old, Kassovitz earned the best director prize at the festival, sparked controversy, and scored a box-office triumph with his anti-police "La Haine" (Hatred).
By comparison, Cannes critics this year were virtually unanimous in panning his third feature film, "Assassin(s)".

Based on a short he made in 1992 with the same title and which was banned to under-16s, it tracks a young loser's (Kassovitz) introduction to murder by a veteran professional (Michel Serrault) with his own twisted code of honour.
Pegged to the hackneyed plot is a heavy-handed message in which the veteran says he has no qualms about his trade because journalists, financiers, and politicians are all murderers.
"We put the 's' in brackets because we are all potential assassins," Kassovitz, who wrote the script with Nicolas Boukhrief, said in the film's press pack.

"What is the difference between an assassin who does his work well and a multinational which throws mercury into rivers? Which is the most dangerous? It's a metaphor which was difficult to accept for (Serrault), I myself don't know if I believe in it," he said.
Running through many scenes are television's mindless games, massacres on the evening news and documentaries on violence in the animal world.
Another murder apprentice shoots a sleeping woman in the back, sits down to watch TV, and then gets up again to fire another few shots into her body.
Denouncing the education youngsters received from society -- pollution, political corruption, sordid television programmes among others --, Kassovitz said:
"At a certain stage, when the shit piles up, the most violent and most scary people in the inner cities are those who are 15 years old because they don't give a damn any more.

"And that's because of the education they have been given and above all because of the example they have been set," said Kassovitz, who added that his previous short had been criticised by some as incitement to murder.

Friday's other competition entry, "She's So Lovely" by American director Nick Cassavetes, is based on a script written by Nick's father, the legendary director John Cassavetes, shortly before his death in 1989.
It stars Sean Penn, John Travolta and Gena Rowlands, who is John Cassavetes' widow.
A passionate couple (Penn and Robin Wright) live a Bohemian life until one of the male partner's escapades lands him in psychiatric hospital.
On his release a decade later, he finds his lover married to a wealthy man (Travolta) in suburban comfort with three children. He promptly forges an outrageous plot to elope with her.

"John gave (the script) to me, and I fell in love with it; mad love at first read. We worked together on it for over a year, before he died. I still wanted to make the film, in fact his death reinforced my desire to do it," Nick Cassavetes recalled.
